kf1.tip: Rank beit knesset, beit tefillah and beit midrash by how much a small town's Jews would miss each if their synagogue closed. Defend each place in a line.
kf1.note: There is no single right order here. A strong answer uses the small-town detail: the lesson says the synagogue is often the sole gathering point for the whole Jewish population, which pushes beit knesset up. Daily prayer and the Amidah make beit tefillah a close rival. Weekly Torah classes make beit midrash matter, but they may feel less urgent. Most put assembly first. The trap is ranking prayer top simply because it is worship.

kf2.tip: Sketch an Orthodox and a Reform synagogue floor plan side by side. Place the bimah, aron hakodesh and ner tamid in each and label what each one is for.
kf2.note: Check your sketch against this. In the Orthodox plan, the bimah should sit in the centre, with the congregation around the reader as in the ancient Temple. In the Reform plan, it should sit at the front, near the ark. Both plans need the aron hakodesh on the east wall, facing Jerusalem, holding the Torah scrolls. The ner tamid goes above the ark in both, showing God's constant presence. Showing the Orthodox women's gallery or mechitza adds strength.

cs1.tip: Argue for and against: the rabbi's role is the biggest Orthodox-Reform difference. Use Jackie Tabick, chazanut and head covering, then decide.
cs1.note: A strong answer weighs three points. Jackie Tabick becoming Britain's first woman rabbi in 1975 shows a deep change in who may lead. Chazanut without instruments on Shabbat, against Reform organs, shapes every service. Head covering is required in one and encouraged in the other. Most decide the rabbi's role matters most, because the lesson names the role of women as a key difference. The trap is listing all three without weighing them.
